name: Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns
title: Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns
answer: Opposing counsel and docket patterns is the study of how lawyers, firms, and courts behave across the public record of a case. It covers motion practice, scheduling, discovery disputes, settlement timing, and the sequence of docket events that precede a ruling. Within litigation prediction and judicial analytics, it connects counsel history to judge history and case type. The site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, which gives a concrete corpus for comparing how AI disputes move through different courts.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Opposing counsel and docket patterns is the study of how lawyers, firms, and courts behave across the public record of a case. It covers motion practice, scheduling, discovery disputes, settlement timing, and the sequence of docket events that precede a ruling. Within litigation prediction and judicial analytics, it connects counsel history to judge history and case type. The site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, which gives a concrete corpus for comparing how AI disputes move through different courts.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on docket data from court electronic filing systems, including PACER and state court portals, plus briefs, orders, and hearing transcripts where available. It needs entity resolution for counsel, law firms, parties, and judges, along with stable case numbers and docket event codes. Storage is usually a relational database or document store with a search index, and a graph layer helps link counsel, firms, judges, and cases. Ingestion runs on a schedule to pull new entries, deduplicate them, and keep the docket timeline current.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts by extracting docket entries, normalizing event types, and linking each appearance to a counsel and firm. From there, analysts compute features such as filing intervals, motion grant rates, continuance frequency, discovery dispute counts, and time to disposition. Those features are compared against the judge's history and the case type, often with simple statistical models or benchmarks rather than deep learning. The site's 29 AI case law precedents can anchor outcome labels for AI-specific disputes, though the sample is small. Validation uses held-out cases, and the work treats correlation as a clue rather than proof of causation.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Docket records are public, but sealed documents, personal data, and protective order material can appear in the same feeds and need careful handling. Provenance matters: record the source court, retrieval date, document type, and whether an entry is a minute order or a full opinion. Counsel pattern analysis can raise ethics and professional responsibility concerns if it becomes harassment, improper profiling, or an unauthorized practice of law. Predictions are not legal advice, and court rules, PACER terms, and data licenses still govern reuse. Bias can enter when some courts have poor digital records or when common names create false matches.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: More courts are publishing structured docket data, which will make counsel-level and team-level patterns easier to measure. Language models may summarize briefs and orders, but docket event prediction will still depend on clean event codes and reliable counsel identity. Expect closer links between docket analytics, conflict checks, outside counsel management, and litigation finance due diligence. As the 148 active AI lawsuits develop, the record will show more counsel-specific patterns in intellectual property and other AI disputes.
